points: * Yglesias' seniority-bas observations al. * Ashman's skepticism about performance pay centers on the documented unreliability of lesson observations (as the Gates Foundation's MET project revealed) and student evaluations as objective measures of effective teaching -- not on the principle of merit pay itself. * Ruggerio's constructivist argument -- explicit instruction develops only routine expertise, discovery learning develops unmeasurable adaptive expertise -- relies on Schwartz and Martin studies that John Sweller critiques for violating the vary-one-thing-at-a-time rule fundamental to controlled experiments. * Ashman notes it is rare these days to find an unequivocal endorsement of constructivist teaching, signaling a research consensus that has moved against discovery-based approaches, while still engaging Ruggerio's evidence directly. * An AI education prompting tool by Hewitt and Sachdeva -- tested and endorsed by Ashman -- converts simple educator questions into detailed prompts for large language models, serving as a practical bridge between AI capability and pedagogical use.
quotes: It is rare the on what Ric constructs k behaviourall "Yglesias makes the point that just because performance pay is imperfect, it does not mean we should stick with the current system which, to his mind, is even worse. This system, replicated across the world, rewards teachers primarily on their length of service. Instead, the evidence for merit-based pay systems spans the range from negligible effects to positive ones.
My worry about observations and student evaluations is that they would push teachers to perform the most fashionable teaching techniques or to try too hard to ingratiate themselves with students.

Essentially, Ruggerio rehearses a familiar-sounding line that although explicit teaching is good for developing routine expertise -- the kind of expertise that might easily demonstrate a strong effect with high grades and high standardized test scores -- constructivist teaching develops adaptive expertise which, conveniently, isn't able to be measured in the same way.

Sweller asks: My questions concern the appropriateness of the control groups used in these studies. If multiple factors are varied simultaneously, as they were in these experiments, does this procedure not break the vary one thing at a time rule essential to all randomized, controlled experiments?

Still, Yglesias has a more pragmatic reason for Democrats in the U.S. to adopt a policy of performance pay for teachers: the wider public approve and so it might help them to get elected. If it's not actively harmful and may even be beneficial, what is there to lose?
